meta.case_name: Rental Cars and Frequent Flyer Miles

prompt.context: Our client is a US airline with a popular frequent flyer mile program. They sell frequent flyer miles through partnerships with credit card companies, hotels, and rental car agencies. While the business overall has been healthy, they have noticed a sharp decline in their frequent flyer miles revenue from the rental car segment: a 50% drop in the last two years.
prompt.question: They have asked us to determine the cause for this loss in revenue, and what they can do to reverse the trend.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the frequent flyer program been in place?
clarifying_info.a: Over 20 years. It was created for competitive advantage and customer retention. This airline was among the very first to have the program, but now almost every airline has one.

clarifying_info.q: How do car rental agencies sell these miles?
clarifying_info.a: An agency advertises that customers can get X frequent flier miles per car rental day. When customers request the miles, they get them and the agency pays the airline for the transaction.

clarifying_info.q: How many rental car agencies are there and how many are partners?
clarifying_info.a: There are 7 major car rental agencies in the country. 5 out of 7 are partners with our client. These 5 agencies comprise 97% of all rental car business in the US.

clarifying_info.q: Has the overall volume of car rentals gone down?
clarifying_info.a: No. The number of cars rented has not gone down and days per rental have not gone down.

clarifying_info.q: Do frequent flyer members prefer renting from partner agencies?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. It is fair to assume that frequent flyer members would strongly prefer to rent a car that came with miles as compared to one that did not.

framework: Define the revenue driver: revenue from rental car segment = (miles sold per transaction) x (price per mile) x (number of transactions)
Investigate each driver: Has transaction volume changed? Has price per mile changed? Has miles per transaction changed?
Root cause: Identify which driver declined and why (rental car agency behavior change)
Solutions: Brainstorm options to reverse the trend, including partnership restructuring
Quantify the best solution: Model willingness-to-pay under exclusive vs. non-exclusive partnership
Other considerations: Agency selection criteria, customer loyalty risk, fixed vs. variable cost accuracy, extension to hotels

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the 50% decline in frequent flyer miles revenue from the rental car segment?
questions.guidance: The candidate should decompose revenue into its drivers. Transaction volume (number of rentals and days per rental) has not declined. The root cause is that the number of frequent flyer miles sold per day has decreased. Rental car companies wanted to lower their own costs per rental by paying less per frequent flyer mile. The airline refused to lower the price per mile. In response, the agencies simply started offering fewer miles per rental day, reducing the total miles purchased from the airline.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm options the airline could pursue to reverse the decline in rental car frequent flyer mile revenue.
questions.guidance: Many logical answers are acceptable. The key insight to reach (prompt if not surfaced): the airline should offer exclusive or semi-exclusive partnerships to a subset of rental agencies rather than partnering with all 5. The value to the selected agencies is a lock on the airline's frequent flyer customers, who strongly prefer renting from partner agencies. This gives the airline pricing leverage.

questions.prompt: Quantify the rental agencies' willingness to pay (WTP) for miles under a semi-exclusive 3-partner model vs. the current 5-partner model. How much could the client benefit? Use the following assumptions: 10 MM rentals/year by frequent flier members; $45 car rental per day on average; average rental is 3 days; ~10% margins on car rentals for agencies before paying for frequent flier miles; currently 5 partners, reduce to 3; current payment from each rental car agency to the airline is $3 per transaction.
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish fixed vs. variable costs. Marginal profit from extra rentals driven by the FF program should use variable costs only (assume all fleet costs are variable for simplicity). Strong candidates will compare total WTP under both models and calculate the incremental revenue opportunity for the airline.

math.setup: Compare agency profit (and hence WTP for miles) under 5-partner vs. 3-partner arrangement. WTP per agency = incremental profit attributable to the FF program. Total airline revenue = sum of WTP across all partners.
steps: A. Current profit to a single rental agency from FF customers: Rentals per agency = 10 MM / 5 = 2 MM rentals/year. Profit per transaction = (10% x $45/day x 3 days) - $3 FF fee = $13.50 - $3 = $10.50. Total variable profit per agency = 2 MM x $10.50 = $21 MM. Equivalently: gross profit before FF fee = 10% x $45 x 3 x 2 MM = $27 MM; FF fees paid = $3 x 2 MM = $6 MM; net = $21 MM.

B. Potential profit to a single agency under 3-partner model: Rentals per agency = 10 MM / 3 = 3.33 MM rentals/year. Gross profit before FF fee = 10% x $45 x 3 x (10/3 MM) = $45 MM. WTP for FF miles = $45 MM (agency would pay up to this to gain those customers, keeping zero incremental profit as upper bound). Incremental WTP vs. current arrangement = $45 MM - $6 MM (current fee) = $39 MM... but compared to net profit baseline: WTP(new) - net profit(current without any fee) is not the right framing. Use: WTP(new per agency) = $45 MM - $21 MM (must at least match current net profit) = $24 MM.

C. Total WTP comparison: WTP(new) = $24 MM x 3 agencies = $72 MM. WTP(old) = $6 MM x 5 agencies = $30 MM (assumes current fee equals max WTP at current arrangement). Incremental revenue to airline = $72 MM - $30 MM = $42 MM.
Key insight: Even capturing half of the $42 MM incremental value would represent a ~67% increase in FF revenue from rental cars ($21 MM / $30 MM).
math.answer: Up to $42 MM in additional annual revenue to the airline from switching to a 3-partner exclusive model. At 50% capture, approximately $21 MM incremental revenue, a ~67% increase over the current $30 MM baseline.

questions.prompt: What other considerations should the airline think about when implementing this strategy?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: (1) How to select the 3 partners — auction, geographic coverage, survey of FF customer preferences, or existing market share among FF customers. (2) Customer loyalty risk — do customers have loyalty to specific rental agencies such that total rentals might shrink under exclusivity? (3) More precise fixed vs. variable cost split for rental agencies — all-variable assumption may underestimate profit impact. (4) Pricing structure — higher price per mile vs. mandating a minimum number of FF miles per rental day. (5) Extension to hotels — if exclusive agreements are profitable in rental cars, could similar deals work with hotel partners?

brainstorming.prompt: What options could the airline pursue to reverse the decline in rental car frequent flyer mile revenue?

categories.name: Partnership restructuring
ideas: Offer exclusive or semi-exclusive partnerships to a subset of rental agencies
Auction exclusive partnership rights to highest bidder
Negotiate minimum miles-per-day floors with partners in exchange for exclusivity

categories.name: Pricing and contract terms
ideas: Mandate that partners advertise a minimum number of FF miles per rental day
Price the new exclusive arrangement based on a higher price per mile
Bundle the rental car partnership with other partnership perks

categories.name: Partner selection criteria
ideas: Select partners based on geographic coverage overlap with airline routes
Survey FF customers for rental car brand preference
Allocate slots based on existing market share among FF customer base

categories.name: Risk mitigation
ideas: Analyze customer loyalty to specific rental brands before finalizing exclusions
Model fixed vs. variable cost split more precisely to stress-test WTP estimates
Pilot exclusive model in one region before national rollout

categories.name: Expansion
ideas: Apply the exclusive partnership model to hotel partners
Explore similar restructuring with credit card partners if revenue trends diverge

categories.name: Customer incentives
ideas: Create tiered mile bonuses for longer rentals to increase days-per-rental
Partner with agencies to offer double-miles promotions to re-engage FF members

recommendation: Switch from the current 5-partner model to a semi-exclusive 3-partner model for rental car agencies. This creates scarcity value for partner status, giving the airline leverage to charge significantly higher fees for miles.
The move could generate up to $42 MM in incremental annual revenue; even at 50% value capture, this represents a ~67% increase in rental car FF revenue, fully reversing the 50% decline.
risks: Some frequent flyer customers may have strong loyalty to excluded rental brands, potentially reducing total miles-generating rentals
The all-variable-cost assumption may overstate agency WTP if fixed fleet costs are not truly variable
Excluded agencies (2 of 5) may retaliate or lobby, creating reputational or regulatory risk
next_steps: Survey frequent flyer members to identify rental car brand preferences and quantify loyalty risk
Conduct a more precise fixed-vs-variable cost analysis for the rental car agencies to sharpen WTP estimates
Design the partner selection process (auction vs. survey-based) and initiate negotiations with the top 3 candidates
Evaluate whether the same exclusive partnership model can be applied to hotel partners
